fields.question: How does LIFT state feedback differ from returning only the sampled token?
fields.answer: A token preserves one discrete choice. State carries continuous top-k distribution information through the shared embedding space. Dedicated state supervision remains necessary; adding any extra vector is not equivalent.
fields.example: Two nearly tied options contain information a single sampled word loses.

fields.question: Can the student loss update LIFT teacher state?
fields.answer: No. Stop teacher gradients; train with token CE and forward KL on the normalized teacher top-k distribution. Inference must use the model's own state.
fields.example: Student errors update the student, not teacher targets to match its mistakes.

fields.question: Why use counterfactual neighbor addresses and a zero sink with hard Lngram v2 lookups?
fields.answer: Binary addresses are discrete and ordinary indexing gives no smooth address gradient. Neighbor comparisons train address choice. GQA reads retrieved tokens alongside a zero sink so irrelevant memory need not be injected.
fields.example: A neighbor may be more useful than the addressed phrase; if neither helps, attend to zero.

fields.question: Why turn hidden states into discrete n-gram addresses?
fields.answer: Recent-state combinations index a memory table in expected O(1); multiple results feed back into the backbone. Explicit addressing has a trainable projection and is not lookup of literal strings only.
fields.example: Two binary hidden-state codes can form a 2-gram key.

fields.question: How do latent addresses differ from text n-gram hashes?
fields.answer: Backbone hidden projections carry context, while text hashes depend directly on discrete input fragments. They do not share an address space or interpretation.
fields.example: The same word in different contexts can yield different latent addresses.

fields.question: Why include a zero sink instead of always using lookup results?
fields.answer: It lets GQA reject irrelevant memory. Counterfactual adjacent addresses supply training signals; the integer index is not ordinarily differentiable.
fields.example: A query can attend to zero to keep an unhelpful lookup out of the residual.

fields.question: Why can loop KV be compressed even when looped Transformer weights are shared?
fields.answer: Loops with shared weights still generate different KV. LLA stores shared low-rank latents and reconstructs loop-specific KV. Rank and error bound savings, and reconstruction costs compute.
fields.example: Four iterations can store a small latent plus four maps rather than four full KV copies, subject to reconstruction quality.

fields.question: How does sharing weights differ from sharing runtime state?
fields.answer: The repeated transform is the same, but KV depends on each loop's hidden inputs. LLA shares a latent while rebuilding each loop's K/V.
fields.example: One machine processing different intermediate materials produces different outputs.

fields.question: What differs between LLA KV compression and reducing parameter count?
fields.answer: Weight sharing reduces parameter storage. Latent compression reduces history cache and adds reconstruction. Their memory scales differ.
fields.example: Cache keeps growing with generated length while model weights remain fixed.

fields.question: What must stay loop-specific when reconstructing KV?
fields.answer: A shared projection produces z, then separate loop matrices U reconstruct K/V. One identical KV for all loops removes the defining difference. The small model is not a post-hoc codec or fused server kernel.
fields.example: Use U¹ and U² on the same z to produce two K outputs.

fields.question: How does MACRO change input computation without changing weights?
fields.answer: A context-conditioned routing program can skip, repeat, or residual-add layers. Feedback updates route probabilities and search selects programs; the backbone is fixed. Use validation, not isolated test gold, for selection.
fields.example: Two prompts can execute different paths through identical layers.

fields.question: Why treat layer execution as a program?
fields.answer: Context-conditioned Markov routes support skip, repeat, and residual-add rather than one fixed order. Feedback updates routes and candidate decoding chooses programs.
fields.example: One input can skip a layer and repeat another.

fields.question: What does routing search change compared with fine-tuning?
fields.answer: It changes how fixed layers execute, not internal parameters. Costs and generalization can differ, and a route is not a new trained backbone.
fields.example: Rearranging blocks differs from reshaping them.

fields.question: Can MACRO greedily concatenate the highest-probability operation at each step?
fields.answer: Not generally. Top-k Viterbi preserves Markov dependencies. Locally greedy choices can miss a better full program; the classification mini-suite is not the paper's scale.
fields.example: A likely repeat now can reduce the score of all later reachable paths.

fields.question: Why pre-encode frequent phrases and fall back to hashed Engram?
fields.answer: An offline model encodes common n-grams into frozen memory; the recipient tries longest-suffix exact lookup. Trainable hash memory covers misses. Projection and contextual gating decide how to use the result, separating offline knowledge cost from online access.
fields.example: A common trigram hits the bank while a rare combination falls back to hashing; either can be gated away.

fields.question: What are the roles of grafting model and recipient?
fields.answer: The grafting model supplies offline intermediate phrase states; the recipient reads this frozen memory online without rerunning the teacher for each phrase.
fields.example: Encode phrases once and look up values later.

fields.question: How does grafted memory differ from Engram trained from scratch?
fields.answer: A pretrained model encodes and freezes the exact bank; longest-suffix lookup precedes trainable hash fallback. Table size alone is not the difference, and local results do not beat equal-parameter Engram.
fields.example: An absent exact phrase uses the explicit hash fallback, not a fabricated value.

fields.question: Which phrase state is stored in the offline bank?
fields.answer: Freeze the final token's hidden state at the specified intermediate grafting layer. The recipient uses separate projection, context gate, and short convolution. End-to-end bank retraining changes the method.
fields.example: Store token four's state for a four-word phrase rather than arbitrarily averaging all four.

fields.question: Why constrain mHC residual mixing to a doubly stochastic matrix?
fields.answer: Repeated unconstrained mixing can amplify deep residual signals. Nonnegative entries and unit row/column sums constrain exchanges while retaining communication. This does not bound growth of the whole nonlinear network.
fields.example: Two streams can mix 0.7/0.3 under both constraints; repeated unconstrained sums may grow quickly.

fields.question: What freedom do multiple residual streams add?
fields.answer: They exchange information dynamically, build attention/FFN inputs, and write back to several streams. Mixing needs constraints because it can amplify depth.
fields.example: Keep different histories and mix as needed rather than using one cumulative vector.

fields.question: Why is mHC more than another normalization layer?
fields.answer: It restricts residual maps to nonnegative doubly stochastic matrices and pre/post maps to nonnegative values. Hidden normalization does not impose those operator constraints.
fields.example: Normalized outputs do not imply row and column sums of one.

fields.question: Are unit row sums enough to validate mHC?
fields.answer: No. Check nonnegativity and unit column sums as well as separate pre/post constraints. A nonexpansive residual mixer does not prove the full nonlinear model is nonexpansive or better trained.
fields.example: Two rows concentrating on one column satisfy row sums but fail column sums.

fields.question: Why vary expert margins rather than add minority class weights?
fields.answer: Margins change score separation geometry; weights scale loss contributions. mild retains full training costs or rewards instead of reducing each to a winner. Estimate margins on training and never read unknown expert costs at inference.
fields.example: Hard minimum-cost labels can discard near-ties involving a specialist.

fields.question: Why can imbalance hurt rare specialist experts?
fields.answer: Broad experts can dominate router learning despite specialists serving particular inputs. Expert-specific margins and full training reward structure retain more information than hard minimum-cost labels.
fields.example: Majority-oriented training may ignore a specialist for a rare question type.

fields.question: What does full expert cost/reward supervision retain over argmin labels?
fields.answer: Argmin keeps only the winner. A cost-based surrogate and expert margins preserve differences and relative score constraints.
fields.example: A close second and an expensive second need not give identical supervision.
